post.name: If humans colonize deep space, it would make sense to adopt metric time.
post.body:
The further we go from Earth and our Sun, the more Earth-based timekeeping begins to break down and becomes less useful as a concept, especially as generations pass. What matters it to Proxima Centauri how many times the Earth has revolved around its local star?

Metric time would provide a universal standard that doesn't depend on any reference to particular rotations and orbits of planets/star systems. Then each system and planet can have their own local timekeeping units, and metric time can enable easy conversions between them.

Using atomic clocks and taking seconds as the primary unit, here's what that could look like:

1 interstellar second = 1 earth second\
1 decasecond = 10 earth seconds\
1 hectosecond = 1⅔ earth minutes (1 interstellar minute)

1 kilosecond = 16⅔ earth minutes\
10 kiloseconds = 2.777 earth hours (1 interstellar hour)\
100 kiloseconds = 1.157407 earth days (1 interstellar day)

1 megasecond = 11.57407 earth days (1 interstellar week)\
10 megaseconds = 16.534391 earth weeks (1 interstellar month)\
100 megaseconds = 38.58024691 earth months (1 interstellar year)

1 gigasecond = 31.709791983764 earth years (1 interstellar decade)\
10 gigaseconds = 1 interstellar century\
100 gigaseconds = 1 interstellar millenium

comment.content: Battletech (attempts) to solve this problem and uses what is called TST (Terran Synchronized Time). Every habitable planet has its rotation broken up into 24 equal time segments aka the TST Hour and all other times chunks are derived from that. These can be vastly different from the Earth Standard or "Metric" time.
